utterances.text: Would you like to have them marked for identification, all three, the report itself and the two annexes?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Sir, do you prepare this report and the two charts independently and reached your conclusions free of any influence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review your report and related charts before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any corrections to make to your report and the main chart listing the post-mortem findings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'll call up exhibit -- exhibit. Document 65 ter 31090A.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, you will see what we're discussing on the screen soon. But in the meantime, I understand these corrections regarded the description of two figures in your report and three dates, as you just mentioned, when the autopsies were performed and these were wrongly recorded in the chart of post-mortem findings; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, consistent with case practice, I would ask that these documents would be marked for identification at this stage pending completion of the cross-examination. And I can list the four 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: If you take them one by one. To start with, the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I would now like to discuss some aspects of your report. Now, I understand from your report that human remains from the Tomasica grave-site arrived at the mortuary facilities in Sanski Most in body bags; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you remember the total number of these body bags?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exactly 400 bags containing human remains. They were there in the mortuary before I arrived, so they were already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And there were also some bags containing artefacts; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- I don't know where there were, I didn't really see them, but there were another 34 bags, I presume, containing artefacts. But in terms of human remains, it was exactly 400 bags.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe the mortuary facilities in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not a proper mortuary by any means. It was a large warehouse in which were many human remains, some relating to Tomasica, and some relating to previous exhumations. The facilities for actually carrying out autopsies is done in a small room, small annex room, with no proper mortuary tables, with just simple wooden tables. There was no running water at the tables as we might expect to do, and there were limited instruments. Despite that, we felt that we would be able to carry out a reasonably full autopsy examination in every case. There were difficulties, but I think we largely overcame them and produced very valid results.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I understand your assessment is -- so did this facility allow, nonetheless, a satisfactory examination of the human remains?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was basic but we could cope with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, generally speaking in your profession, there are any principles, protocols or best practices guiding the work of a pathologist and that you would follow in your work when carrying out post-mortem examinations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all pathologists will work to a principle of initially having some background information of the case, then looking at a body externally for perhaps clothing, other items. Looking again at the external surface of the body for different findings, injuries, changes after death, et cetera, and then proceeding to do an internal examination. Possibly after that, taking appropriate samples of tissue or fluids, and at the end of all that, bringing everything together into a report and conclusions. So that's a standard procedure which would be adopted worldwide. Clearly different situations would have a refinement of that, but that would be the general principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you remember describing this process and the methodology that you would follow for post-mortem examinations in your other reports related to grave-sites in Bosnia, your reports that were previously admitted in evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your work as a pathologist at the Sanski Most mortuary, did you and the Bosnian pathologists follow these basic pathologist principles and protocols regarding the way to conduct autopsies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some differences, it has to be said, from the procedures that we had adopted at the specific ICTY missions previously. This was being run by the Bosnian authorities. And here there was a separation of different stages of looking at the body. Previously the pathologist would be very much in charge really from the moment the body bag was first opened and would view or -- or have an oversight of the procedure throughout. In Sanski Most, other people initially opened the body bags, examined the body, cleaned the body, removed the clothing, and the pathologist really only came in at the end -- well, not at the end, but part way along to actually carry out the physical autopsy. The other difference is that we had no radiology support in Sanski Most as we had had in previous missions. But, in terms of looking at the body, removing it from a body bag, the external examination, the internal examination, the photography, removing of samples was all the same as previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can maybe go to -- oh, I see we don't have -- okay. If we can have the report on the screens, please, and this is marked for identification with P7443. And if we can please have page 2 of this document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, this part of your report refers to the procedure in the mortuary, something that you were just discussing, and I see in the middle of the page three bullet points, 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So from what you just said, do I understand correctly that what you described in points 1 and 2 was carried out by other personnel working at the mortuary, while point 3, the one regarding autopsies or -- was carried out by pathologists. Can you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just inquire. You have your report before you at this moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and you are consulting that rather than anything on the screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. I just have it here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. We just like to know exactly what you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you said you analysed a total of 400 body bags. Can you tell us how many bodies did you analyse out of these bags of human remains.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies had been labelled at the grave-site by those exhuming and they had been given a sequential number, and at the end of that, had been given either a letter, a T, to denote what they thought or they considered a whole or largely complete body, or a D, referring to what they considered as a body part. I'll come back to that definition. Or, finally, a small number were given a letter GB, meaning general bag. This is when isolated bones were found in the grave area which could not be associated with particular bodies and were put together as what you call a general bag, GB, general bag. So they would be a general bag for one particular area of the body, another one for another area, another one for another area. So, in total, out of these -- so this made up 400 bags of human remains. 275 had been labelled as complete, or largely complete bodies, T; and 125 had been labelled as body parts. Now, I'm including in that the 13, 13 general bags. So 125 of either body parts or general bags.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And so I understand you worked and analysed both the bags containing largely complete bodies and those containing body parts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We looked at every -- every bag.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go back to the definition of body versus that of a body part. You said you wanted to go back to that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I developed this later on in the report, but essentially it is very much common sense what to anybody would be a body or most of a body, I think everybody would recognise. Perhaps there might be a forearm missing or a foot missing, but it is still in all intents and purposes a body. A body part would -- usually most people would think of as perhaps part of a leg, a skull, a forearm or a hand, just a part of a body, and that's easy to understand. There's a group in between in which perhaps the whole trunk is there but missing the legs and/or the arms. Now, it's individual judgement, at the grave-site a number of these -- these states of bodies had been labelled as a body part. In the mortuary, I felt -- well, in my interpretation of the findings, I felt I could -- some of these large body parts actually, I think, constituted a body. And I've added 18 of them, of the body parts, to the 275 proper bodies to make a total of 293, which I regard as a pathologist as separate individuals which I was able to interpret or examine and analyse. So that's -- it may sound slightly complicated, but, in essence, in the end, I have for the purposes of report analysed 293 - that's 275 plus 18 - 293 bodies for -- in terms of looking at injuries and other findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, again, in your last sentence, when you refer to 293 bodies, this definition does not necessarily refer to complete bodies, to fully complete bodies.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, did the remains exhumed at the Tomasica site present any particular or unique figure that you might want to discuss or bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were all struck - pathologists and anthropologists and others - by how well preserved many of these bodies were. These were bodies which had reportedly been in the ground for up to 21 years. We would have expected most of these bodies to be reduced to a skeleton, but, in fact, a large number of them had not -- a lot of soft tissue on the bones, in sometimes a great amount so that the complete shape of the body was still there. You could recognise facial features. One person we could even see a tattoo on their arm. And this was quite remarkable. I'd never seen or none of us had come across this degree of preservation of bodies before. It's a process in the -- normally the body after death starts to decompose, and essentially the tissues will break up and liquify and you'll be reduced to a skeleton. Here, we have a -- there are variants and this is one of them. Here a variant is that because of the particular circumstances, the fatty tissues in the body don't turn to liquid but instead form into a very hard substance like soap. That's a substance called adipocere and it is very persistent. So you can imagine all the fatty tissues of the body just -- instead of disappearing, just stay there and become very, very hard. So that's what we had in many of the bodies here, not all of them, and some of them had indeed been reduced to a skeleton and some were part way -- a mixture of both. I can't completely explain why that should be. But I think the reason why we had the adipocere here, this hardening, and the tissue preservation was probably a combination of the depth of the burial, the type of the soil. It requires a degree of moisture, maybe the soil was slightly alkaline instead of acid, and maybe other factors as well. But it was very unusual. It was striking.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, and what significance, if any, the degree of preservation of bodies exhumed from Tomasica had on your work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preserving the bodies and holding them together, it made identification of injuries that little bit easier, in terms of tracks -- bullet tracks particularly, so we could see it going through soft tissue and into bone. Because in skeletonised remains, the bones will just all come apart, but here we could still actually see very straightforward tracks. So that that was the main benefit of that. It also -- any bullets in the body would be held in the tissues, embedded in the tissues, whereas in a skeletonised body, they'll just fall out. So that was the two advantages: Bullet tracks and actually finding bullets. The disadvantage is that this tissue can sometimes become very, very hard and it becomes very difficult to open up the body and to work with it. It also made the bodies heavy, and undoubtedly, the weight of all the bodies on top of each other undoubtedly produced fractures after death of particularly the ribs. So -- any way, this preservation was a remarkable feature in the bodies. And one other feature, in probably entirely academic interest, was a blue colour which kept appearing on the surface of these bodies and on the bones which I have not mentioned in my report but subsequently worked out as a specific mineral which forms in soils with lots of iron in them. A combination of the tissues of the body and the iron produces this chemical called vivianite which makes the surface of the body blue. It is probably entirely academic interest, but it was another feature of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can the Court officer please call up 65 ter 32667. Your Honour, the photograph that is about to appear on the screens is one of a set of photographs taken at the Sanski Most morgue by photographer Claudia Heinermann in October 2013 and she has agreed to them being used in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at the body in the centre of the photograph. Does this show the degree of preservation that we were just discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. If I can just interpret it for people. The head is towards the right end of the screen and the feet are clearly to the left-hand side. He still has trousers on, but if you look at the upper half of the body, you can see brown and white tissue which is this adipocere. It is very dry and hard. You can see his bent arm in the lower half of the photograph. You can almost see the fingers still there. So you can see how identifiable these remains are as bodies. In contrast, if you look at the body just above, where the bulk of the tissues have gone and all you're seeing are the bones, there's still a little tissue towards the right towards the top of the body, towards the top of the screen, but largely skeletonised. So a mixture of degrees of preservation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And on the first body you commented upon, the one well preserved, we can also still see the clothes that this individual was wearing; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have -- well, there's still some clothing still on the lower part of his body, his trousers. There's a shirt down -- taken already off, down to the left-hand side. The body above, the clothes will be in that black bag. They have already been taken off and washed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this photograph as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32667 receives number P7447.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the clothes, the clothing, what can you tell us about the clothes found on the bodies exhumed from Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the clothing that we found -- most people did have clothing on. All the clothing was just ordinary clothing that people would wear - shirts, sweatshirts, short-sleeve shirts, trousers, et cetera. Some people had suit jackets, some people had work jackets or dungarees, but it was mostly sort of casual clothes with footwear as well. Some people did have a few -- a few people did have what to me was an excessive amount of clothing, so perhaps two or more jackets, two or more pairs of trousers. One of the three women had an enormous number of clothes on, but generally this was fairly light clothing. Specifically, no military clothing whatsoever. And I include amongst that the footwear which was all of a light -- generally of a light nature and not boots or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask one little question, sir. Sir, this might be outside your area, but are you able to tell us why, after 21 years, the clothing is still there also? I mean, when you look at the skeletonised remains, the body -- not only is the soft tissue gone but you don't -- you also don't see the clothing. Is there an explanation why on the one that is not skeletonised clothing is also still there, hasn't meshed into the tissue or dissolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there's two issues there. Of the two bodies that we saw, both of them did have clothing and it's just one has -- they have been removed. Yes, you're correct. I mean, it's remarkable how clothing does survive in the ground. Clearly we did not see the clothing that did not survive and that might be a specific type. Certain types of clothing, as I recall, denim jeans don't survive very well and any jeans that we found were generally tattered. So I think it's a -- it's the specific type of cloth will help the preservation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move now to the causes of death that you observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can I please call up P7443, marked for identification. And if we go to page 8 of the English and 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, what did you observe as the most frequent cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can summarise it just in the first three lines there, that I found that the vast majority of the people in this grave-site had been shot, many of them just once, one man unusually nine times, but mostly a small number of times. Wounds to the head were a dominant feature, a regular common feature to find wounds to the head and particularly to the back of the head. And most injuries were from high-velocity weapons. So, in summary, just about everyone had been shot, and a very common finding was a bullet wound, bullet injury, to the back of the head. That's a broad statement, and then I then analysed it in a lot more detail --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll go into that detail.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll go through that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I see also in the second paragraph that you discuss -- you found gun-shot injuries in all but ten cases, that is 283, representing the 97 per cent. And I guess this applies to the 293 bodies that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're now forgetting the body parts and we're dealing only with the 293 full or largely complete bodies. Of these 293, 283 had gun-shot injuries, so that's 97 per cent. The other ten we can deal with at the end, but by far the majority had gun-shot injuries. I then look at the number of gun-shot injuries that each of these people had. In other words, had they been shot once, twice, three times, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, you're now commenting on Table 3, I take it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Table 3. The commonest situation was that a person had been shot just once. Next commonest, they had been shot twice. Then a little, little less, shot three times, and then greatly decreasing after that. One man, and only one man, had been shot nine times. One eight times, et cetera. So most people had been shot once, twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Were you also able to make an estimate of the minimum number of bullets that were fired in total on the bodies exhumed from the Tomasica grave-site for what you could observe, of course?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, therefore, looking at the gun-shot injuries and I've worked out a total of 709 gun-shot injuries to these people. Now I think that will be an underestimate of shots, and there are a number of reasons for saying it's an underestimate. Partly that is because in, say, the trunk of the body, if we found a bullet damage to a bone, say the left collar bone, and another one to a rib at the right-hand side, it's conceivable that could all be the one shot travelling across the body. Alternatively, it could be two individual shots striking the body. Sometimes it was easy to tell the difference, but if I was in any doubt, I would give the benefit of the doubt to saying it was just the one shot. Similarly, if a gun-shot injury, say, in the chest and an injury also in an arm, I gave the benefit of the doubt that that was actually the same track, so the bullet hitting the arm first and then going into the chest. It may well have been two separate shots, but I gave, as I say, the benefit of the doubt to it being the same. So these various arguments, overall I think this is probably an underestimate of the shots, but a fairly reasonable assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So the total of 709 gun-shot injuries to these people that you just discussed, it's a conservative assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And now if you can give us a bit more details about the process of identifying gun-shot injuries. You were going into this detail already in your previous answer. If you can elaborate on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the injuries we found were caused by high-velocity weapons. That is, when a bullet leaving the rifle at a very high speed, with lot of energy, and when it hits the body, it loses that energy very quickly and causes a great deal of damage, particularly to the bones, so you get a shattering effect. Most of the time we were analysing -- for gun-shot injuries we were looking at the bones because that is the easiest thing to find. Often we would find a nice round entrance hole in the bone and some fractures shattering round about and that to us was a classic -- almost 100 per cent had to be a gun-shot injury. We could say that with certainty. Other times perhaps you had the same shattering effect but maybe not the complete hole because parts of the bone were missing. But to our mind, it was difficult to think of anything else which could have caused such a degree of shattering of the bone so we were happy to say that these were probable gun-shot injuries. And, finally, there was a situation in perhaps it was just a simple fracture of a bone or simple damage which could have been a gun-shot injury, slightly unusually, or could have been caused by something else, and I might call that a possible gun-shot injury. Now in my analysis, I didn't consider the possible ones. I only considered the definite and the probable gun-shot injuries. As I say, for these probable ones, the degree of damage was -- I couldn't think of any other explanation for these, and I think it's highly likely that they were gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And we will see the differences in reporting definite, probable, or possible gun-shot injuries in -- when looking at the chart where you have recorded the autopsy findings. But, yes, so I understand that the -- at page 5 and 8 of your report you explain this qualification that you gave of a definite, a probable, and a possible gun-shot injury.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in the count, I understand you considered only the definite and probable ones.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, what can you tell us about the distribution of the gun-shot injuries that you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is now looking at what parts of the body were damaged by these shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe we can go to page 9 of the English, 11 of the B/C/S, and look at Table 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir, I would ask you to comment on this table within the context of my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So as I say, we're looking now at what parts of the body were damaged by these bullets. The commonest injuries -- most of the injuries were found in the trunk. In other words, that's the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis area, that's the trunk of the body. Which is not surprising because that's the biggest part of the body surface area. Having said that, a surprising number, a surprisingly high number of shots were to the head and the neck, but particularly the head; and correspondingly, a relatively low number were to the legs, which actually form quite a substantial part of the body. If you then look onto the diagram in Figure 3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, you're now referring to Figure 3, the diagram showing a human body.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and what I've done here is to put the body into three areas: The head and neck; the trunk from the neck down to the pelvis and including the arms; and thirdly, the legs. Now, in a normal body, the head only forms 9 per cent of the body surface. In the normal body, the trunk and arms form 54 per cent of the body surface, and the legs form 36 per cent. So if you look at the gun-shot injuries - and this is the black figures on the left-hand side - 58 per cent of the shots to the body were to the trunk which roughly fits in with that being that proportion of the body surface area. But instead of only the 9 percent in the head, we had 35 per cent of the shots, all the shots, were to the head, and a corresponding lack of injuries to the lower legs. This is if the shots -- these were shots with just a random distribution of shots. So it looked to me there was a specific -- the head had been -- was a specific target area, if you like. It certainly predominated. There was far more shots to the head than you would expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So do I understand your evidence correctly, that the percentages that you present in Figure 3 - and I mean those in black, in bold - these would not be compatible with random distribution of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if -- if a gun was being fired randomly at people, then you would expect shots to hit the body roughly in proportion to the body area, so the figures we've got here rather go against that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one follow-up question. The relevance of all this would be clear if, in combat situations, soldiers would shoot randomly at other bodies and that the situation of the bodies would be such that you could hit them randomly. I'm thinking, for example, about a soldier lying on the ground with a rifle, raising his head a little bit higher in order to find a target when lying down and trying to shoot --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which would expose his head in a way, I would say not randomly, to any fire coming from the other side. Is -- of course, I'm asking myself what the relevance is of your observations and developed these thoughts, and I'd like to hear your comment as an expert on relevance and such situations as I described.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's entirely a reasonable suggestion about the head being struck. As we'll see later on, in that particular situation, you would imagine, then, that most shots coming to that soldier would be to the front or the top of the head. In fact, the bulk of the shots were to the back of the head, so that's one point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, we have not gone to that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but it is presented here as -- that there's a relevant difference just on the basis of the body surface and I was wondering what the relevance of that was, apart from relevant factors found elsewhere, not the head. But the back of the head is, of course, not the same as the head in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know what situation these people were in, but the -- if you imagine the situation when everybody was standing up at the time, then it just seems a little odd that so many shots were to the head. But I quite agree that you can envisage a situation in which the person was -- were lower down and only the head was exposed. That's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the benefit of having dealt with other cases in the Balkans, it did strike me how many -- how much commoner it was in these bodies than in other sites that I've dealt with the injuries to the head, and I've labelled that in Table 5 just to show --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe we can move to the discussion on the direction of fire. So if we can go to page 11 of the English and 13 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So that we can continue the discussion about the direction of fire and the portion, for example, of the head where you observed the highest number of gun-shot injuries. Sir, can you comment and Table 6 and Figure 6 together.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is looking at the particular part of the body surface, whether it's the front or the back or the top or the side, et cetera, and there are various ways we can try and work that out. The head being the easiest, if we look at that, of all the shots to the head, 45 per cent of them were to the back of the head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have the corresponding page in B/C/S with respect to Table 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the next page, page 14 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So 45 per cent of all shots to the head were to the back of the head. Only 17 per cent were to the front of the head, and then 27 per cent were either to the top or the side of the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 20 per cent or 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 plus 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Plus 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 plus 9. And 11 per cent we were not able to say really because of the amount of damage and parts missing. So the commonest finding was a gun-shot injury to the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what about the trunk? What was the assessment about the direction of fire with regard to that part of the body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trunk is less able -- we're less able to be certain about it, but of the shots that we could analyse for direction, almost 60 per cent, 59 per cent, were, we felt, to the back of the body. I'm meaning really from the outer part of the ribs backwards I would count as the back of the body. A lot of times we weren't able to say, but where we were able to say, the majority were to the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And as we are on this page, we should go back to page 13 on the B/C/S, can you explain also how you would determine the direction of fire, and in doing that, you can -- could you comment upon Figures 5A and 5B that we see on the top of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In remains like these, we try and analyse direction of fire by the specific damage caused in the bone. So a bullet striking bone, the very first surface it hits will produce a round hole. As it comes out of the other side of that bone, then the shape of the hole is wider. It's sort of funnel-shaped. It's a process we call bevelling. And by looking that, we can tell which direction a bullet was going through a bone. So we can do that with the head, we can do it with a rib, we can do it with an arm or the pelvis, et cetera. The head is the easiest because the skull is thick and retains these features. So in that way that's how we can tell direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will go more into the details of the damages or the effects of these gun-shot injuries on the bones after the break, because we see we are about to break. But before we finish with these photos, can you tell us where this photo is taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 5A and 5B?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my own photographs of one of the cases, 275T. It is a skull which initially was in multiple fragments but which has now been glued together. And you can see in 5A, the left-hand picture, you will see the entrance hole, this round circular in -- right in the centre, that is where the bullet has gone in. As well as producing a round hole, it has produced fractures above, below, and to the sides. Now, the photograph B, on the right, is actually the other side of the skull. So the bullet has gone in the right side, it's just above the right ear effectively, slightly higher up, and it has come out the left side of the head. Where a high-velocity bullet strikes the -- particularly the skull, it causes a fairly neat entrance hole, but as it comes out the other side, it causes enormous shattering of the bone, and all you're left is usually a large defect where the bone is in multiple pieces or is actually lost. And what we're looking at here is the left side of the skull.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So on the right-hand side photo, the red arrow indicates --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the inner surface of the hole seen in the left-hand picture. Now, if you're able to zoom that picture up, at the red arrow you would actually see the bevelling effect in the surface of that entrance hole.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a complication here because in the skull we're talking about two exits, we're talking about the exit of the initial -- the initial surface of the bone but then we're also talking about the exit of the bullet through the whole head. That's why -- or perhaps the wording is slightly confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That red arrow, the inside of that has a sort of funnel-shaped -- and that tells us clearly what direction that bullet was travelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Mr. Clark, we'd like to see you back after 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, are you on track? Your estimate was two hours, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you've used a little bit over one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm on track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, we discussed your findings and observations regarding the numbers of gun-shot injuries, the distribution of gun-shot injuries, and the direction of fire. I want to move now to your observations regarding the weapons used to inflict the injuries. And so my first question would be: Were you able to tell which type of weapon inflicted the gun-shot injuries that you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our view, the majority of injuries were caused by high-velocity weapons. I've explained earlier what I mean by that term. It really is a weapon in which the bullet is fired with a very high speed, a lot of energy, and when it strikes the body, causes a great deal of damage. We were able to say that on the basis of the type of damage found in the bone -- found in the body, particularly the shattering of the bones, but also in actually finding remnants of typical high-velocity bullets still in the bodies. So from a combination of these two, the majority of injuries were caused by high-velocity weapons. At the same time, there was a small number of cases in which it was clear handguns, pistols, revolvers, et cetera, had been used, and that was obvious either from finding handgun bullets in the bodies or by finding bullet injuries which didn't have the same degree of shattering that you get from the high-velocity weapon and suggested more to us the use of a lower velocity such as a handgun.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I understand from your answers that there are visible differences between injuries or trauma caused by high-velocity weapons and those caused by handguns on the bones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe if we look at Figures 7A and 7B - this would be page 12 of the English and page, I believe, 15 of the B/C/S - this would give us a visual aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And I would ask you, sir, to comment on these two photographs. And, again, if you can first tell us where these photographs were taken.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are just two random photographs taken from the cases. The one on the left-hand side is a gun-shot injury of the face and the top of the spine. And just to orientate you, the lower jaw is normally a horse-shoe shaped bone and you can see the front of the jaw is right at the foot of the photograph. And then it goes back on the left side with the teeth there. The right side of the jaw is -- there's a large gap there, and that's where a bullet has gone and it has gone backwards and it's hit the spine. And normally that vertebra at the top of the spine is solid. Here it is shattered into multiple pieces, and that's very typical of a high-velocity bullet going through the jaw and into the vertebra. On the right -- the picture on the right-hand side, 7B, this is a bullet going through the femur, that's the thigh bone, on the left thigh. It's causing a hole but also multiple fractures round about. Now, that's typical of a damage caused by a high-velocity weapon. If that was a handgun, all you would probably see would just be a round hole with minimal fracturing round about it. It'd just be a straight round hole. Here you've got lots of fracturing and fragmentation and that's how we can tell the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now move to page 15 of the English and 18 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, while this is coming up, I understand there were also a number of unascertained cases where not convincing cause of death could be found; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 12 cases in which we could not come to a conclusion as to the cause of death. Two of these did have a gun-shot injury but in a part of the body which we felt would not necessarily cause death. One was to the jaw, and I think the other one was to a shoulder. Now, they were definitely gun-shot injuries but I couldn't necessarily conclude that that person would have died from that. So that kind of were two of them --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I take it you're commenting on Table 7 which summarizes the unascertained causes of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Other times we found no gun-shot injuries in what we examined. But in a number of these cases, a part of the body was missing - perhaps a head or a leg - in which there could well have been a gun-shot injury, but in the part of the body we had there was no gun-shot injury. So these account for most of these unascertained cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, again, these 12 would be out of the 293 bodies that you -- you discussed in your report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So we found of these 293 people, 96 per cent of them, so most of them, died from a gun-shot injury and only a small number we couldn't establish, really, how they had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I would now like to discuss with you some examples from the two annexes or charts annexed to your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So if we can please have P7444 MFI on the screens. And we can just start with page 1 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this chart, this table, now on the screens?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So this is the first annex, the large -- larger chart on the post-mortem findings to your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can look at this first page of the annex, and if you can please guide us through this chart and how to read it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first column under case number is the number given to the body bag at the Tomasica site by the exhumation team. So we have -- they're in sequential numbers. So 13, and that would be a T at the end, meaning a whole body. The next one is a D. Now, this is one of the 18, this is one of the 18 that I've added to a kind of whole bodies. The first part of this annex, the first 80, almost 90 pages are these 293 cases. It's not the body parts. The body parts come at the end of the annex. So these principal cases are the 293 cases which I've analysed. Most of them Ts, already recognised as bodies, but 18 of them are these body parts, which I've upgraded to a body although kept the D letter. So that's what these -- the first column refers to. And it goes from 13T up to, I think, 420 or so T towards the end. The second column, there's three levels there. The first date is the date of the post-mortem examination or the autopsy examination. The second is the date when the body was exhumed from the grave, clearly at a time earlier. And the third, in italics, is the part of the grave-site from where the body was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And a small clarification. It is to this column that you made a couple of corrections in the table of corrections that we looked at earlier on; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was simply the date of the -- that the autopsy, a figure had been wrongly put down.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My fault in doing that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Please continue. Maybe can you comment on the -- yeah, on the fourth, fifth, and sixth column as well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the other columns are fairly -- well, the third one is self-evident it's the sex and the estimated age of the individual. Sometimes a little bit more specific. The fourth column are the clothing, the clothing that the person was wearing, and I have only included the main outer clothing, not underwear or socks, et cetera, for clarity. Plus any other items either around the body or in their possession, so car keys, ID cards, spectacles, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And one point of clarification, the observations in this part, in the observations regarding clothing and artefacts, were those that you personally made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the autopsy we -- the pathologist then examined all the clothing and all the items, the possessions with that body, so we directly saw these and logged them all. The fifth column is just a general description of the remains, the completeness of the body, so it was a largely -- a complete body or largely complete body, what was missing, was it reduced to a skeleton, was there a lot of adipocere, a lot of tissue, et cetera, et cetera. So that is a general description there. The fifth column, gun-shot injuries, lists -- sorry, sixth column. It lists all the gun-shot injuries. GSI means gun-shot injury. Now, most of them are, in my mind, confident gun-shot injuries or what I think are very clear gun-shot injuries. Where I thought the injury was probable or possible, then that is specifically added.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now with regard to that, can we zoom in on case 015D, just the second in the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The right side of the line or the left side?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The left side of the line. Thank you, Your Honour. Including the part on the description of the gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is the next column.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This needs to move along a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I wanted you -- yeah, to ask if you could explain the difference between the two bullet points listed in the gun-shot injuries column.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on 15D.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have, first of all, a gun-shot injury, a definite gun-shot injury of the head. The entrance hole is at the back of the head in what's called the left occipital region - that's just to the left of the back of the head - which had also damaged the upper bone of the spine, the C1 vertebra. The bullet had come out opposite, towards the front of the right side of the head in the right temporal region, and also damaging the right side of the jaw. So that was a gun-shot injury, definite gun-shot injury entering the back of the left side and coming out on the right side. Secondly, I'd found a gun-shot injury -- well, what I assumed -- said was a probable gun-shot injury of the right forearm, with damage to the lower end of one of the bones there. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, although I listed that as a gun-shot injury, there could be the possibility that that is somehow connected with the injury to the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the forearm, the arms are very movable, and you could envisage perhaps the forearm up against the head and being struck as the bullet exits or conceivably the forearm was round at the back of the head at the entrance point. Generally for injuries to the forearms, I consider very much whether they could all be part of an injury elsewhere to the body and kind of almost assumed that they were. So again, a slightly potential underestimate of the number of shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we move to the right-hand side part of this table --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Clark, in your oral testimony today you talked about the gun-shot injury, a definite one, and that the entrance was at the back in the left region. Now, the report says with probable entrance. You didn't repeat that. Therefore, I'm wondering why you told us the entrance hole is at the bottom of the head whereas in the report it says the probable entrance is at the back. And could you also explain -- apparently the probability is not only related to whether these are gun-shot injuries, yes or no, but apparently also as far as the -- in this case, the direction of fire is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very valid point. Sometimes if we could see a hole, a proper circular entrance hole, that was clearly the entrance. Sometimes there wasn't that hole but there was the damage, the fragmentation round about. In this particular case, there would have been a lot of damage to the back of the head. I think we were more confident about where the exit had been, just by the nature of the damage. And so lining up, because bullets travel in a direct line, we worked out that the entrance was very likely to have been at the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the same kind of probability you told us about earlier, that is, that although the direct evidence isn't there, that you couldn't give any other explanation as the one you gave as the probable cause of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. I mean, in this particular case, there was clearly an exit here, the entrance could not have been at the top of the head, it couldn't have been at the front, just from the nature of the exit damage, and that's why we have found damage at the back of the head and felt that that was the probable area. The left occipital covers quite a big area so it's -- it was in that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we move to the right-hand side part of this table, I want to have a look at the last column together with the column on gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you comment about the minimum number of shots reported in the -- in the last column, cause of death, and reconnect these to the discussion of gun-shot injuries in the relevant column?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the column of gun-shot injuries you will see that I have listed two gun-shot injuries: One to the head and one to the forearm. On the basis that the injury to the forearm could well have been in the same track as the one to the head, I thought that's a minimum number of one shot to the body. It could have been two, but I worked on the basis of a minimum number and that was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now move to page 76 of the English, and in the B/C/S this starts at page 79.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you to comment on case number 371T, for your reference on the chart that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe we can first zoom in on the left-hand side part of the column, including the gun-shot injuries column. The left-hand side part of the chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the man with -- who had nine shots. Most of these were to the head where we found extensive fracturing of the skull and no less than six bullets, either whole or fragmented bullets, within the head. This was certainly a case which was very difficult, as you can imagine, to reconstruct the skull, but we found a bullet, some bullet entrance holes, exit damage, and, as I say, portions of at least six separate bullets in the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you also found -- did you also find the bullet?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was these portions of bullets, either a complete bullet or portions of bullets. But it was clearly items from six separate bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I see there's a text in green in the gun-shot injuries column. Can you tell us what does the regular green font indicate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we zoom in in the B/C/S version in the same way as in the English and leave out the right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, from column 1 to column 6, and leave out column 6 -- 7. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Most of the discussion and the part in green font in B/C/S would be on the next page, page 80. Maybe we can move to page 80 in the B/C/S and zoom in the -- on the column that has the green font. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, should I repeat my question --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I compiled this chart, really for my own benefit, any mention of a bullet I've put in green so that I can immediately -- it highlights to me immediately. If I see green, there's discussion of a bullet or bullet fragment. Where that referred to a bullet or fragment which was actually found in the tissues of the body, in a bone, or in the soft tissue, wherever, then it's within that individual -- the description of the -- that particular gun-shot injury. But you will also see --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, there's also some green italics, so if you can explain the difference between the two fonts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very last one, if it is in italics, this refers to bullets or bullet jackets which had been recovered by others during the washing of the body which were made available to us to look at subsequently. I just note them. I haven't counted them in any analysis or based anything on them, but just to say that they were bullets or bullet jackets or fragments of bullets recovered from the remains during washing by other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Again, to sum up, the regular green font indicates bullets located in the body and therefore I assume by you, by pathologists?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we found. That, yes, we found.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. If we can move to the right-hand side part of the table just to have a look at the final column describing the causes of death and the minimum number of bullets, and if you can briefly comment on that. It is self-explanatory but just about -- a comment maybe about the minimum number of shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: This in English would be the next page, 77, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked out that this man, because he had six shots to the head, I worked out there were other shots to the trunk and one to the left upper arm. Again, a shot to the upper arm could well be associated with one of the shots to the chest so I counted all that as one. In total, I estimated that he had been shot at least nine times, so the minimum number of shots is nine there. All, to my mind, by a high-velocity weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are we on the right page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're not --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes -- in the English it is the very top of the chart. It's a little section that continues from the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cause of death here was given as gun-shot injuries to the head and chest because any bullets going through these areas would be very rapidly fatal. But you'll see in the very -- the three arrow points at the base -- it's actually only one, you've missed the top one in your -- on the screen. It's on the previous page. But I've listed all the injuries to all parts of body whether or not they contributed to the death. So cause of death here was gun-shot injuries to the head and chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Then we discussed how you also encountered cases of injuries caused by handguns.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So if we can move to page 43 of this document and 47 -- 43 of the English and 47 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you to comment on case number 230T and 227T. They appear on the same page. Maybe -- let's go to 227T, which is in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the three women in the grave. She had a gun-shot injury to the head with the entrance just above, behind the left eye, and the exit on the right side of the head towards the back. In other words, above the right ear. The fracturing associated with these, the entrance and exits, was relatively minimal compared to most other cases and, for that reason, I wondered about the use of a handgun because it's a lower energy and didn't cause quite so much damage. So I've concluded that probable -- probable handgun cause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Before moving to the right-hand side part of the chart, I see the description -- can you comment on the clothing artefact? I see a very dense description of what this individual was wearing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had a lot of -- lot of clothing, indeed. Multiple layers of blouses, trousers, nightdress, et cetera. It just seemed to go on and on. So she was somebody who certainly had far more clothing than you would --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think you referred to this case at the very beginning of today's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Was this the same person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly mentioned somebody with lot of excess clothing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we could move to the right-hand side part of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, yes, we see in the cause of death description a handgun and the -- yeah, the same is true for case 230T.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 230T, I was a bit more confident that this definitely was a handgun, again, because the bullet-holes were so regular and lacked the fragmentation. This again was another woman and there were two entrance holes in the skull.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Before we leave this page, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's found on the next page, I take it, where the handgun is without --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the word "probable." It's on page 44, the final conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is not on our screen now. It's the very top line. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir -- where is it? Yeah. If we look at the column: Other injuries or findings, can you explain what the hashtag sign indicates?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means a fracture. That's a universal -- the term universally adopted by medical personnel as a shortcut for a fracture.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now move to page 93 of this document, 93 of the English, and B/C/S page 108.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to bodies, we discussed -- you told us how you and your colleagues also analysed body parts. Now can you describe your work on the body parts and the differences and challenges encountered, if any.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We paid as much attention to the body parts as to the whole bodies, did them in turn. Clearly they were easier to look at in terms of there was one only small part of the body, so we were able to get through them more quickly. Some of these body parts would be, as I say, just maybe a whole arm or an arm bone or a foot. Sometimes a mixture of bones from skull, chest, et cetera. So we went through these in the same way - sometimes they had clothing, sometimes they didn't - looked for gun-shot injuries and any other damage, tried to give a cause of death. Now, as you can imagine, the majority of these there was no injury to -- to them, and the cause of death was given as unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We see that if we move to the right-hand side part of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In both languages, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And for the record, yes, starting from this page, page 93 of the English and 108 of the B/C/S, the chart discusses the additional body parts while the first part of it regards the -- all the bodies, the principal cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, sir, just some brief questions about the last document part of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if we can have P7445, MFI, on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. We can now see the summary chart or list of post-mortem findings that you also attached to your report. And again I would ask you to please comment on the chart and to briefly explain the information in it and what -- what type of searches this facilitates, if any.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a just an abbreviated version of the previous document. It doesn't give any more information than is in the previous -- the main document but is perhaps easier to get an immediate overview of the findings. So, again, the case number, the sex of the person, the age range, an indication of -- a little bit more clearly of the -- whereabouts in the grave they came from, which gives an overall picture of working round the grave, so all the 1s and 2s and 3s are roughly together. Then a cause of death, including the unascertained. Then a table showing the injuries, any gun-shot injuries to the body whether or not they contributed to the cause of death or not. That's GSI injuries. And finally, final column is the minimum number of shots. This is the figures on the left-hand side of that column. Followed by either H-V for high velocity or HG, in brown, for handgun or a query if we didn't know. And some of them will have an asterisk which indicates that there was bullets or bullet fragments found associated with that body. And very occasionally there's a wavy sign, which indicates that there was a cartridge case.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think we see that on the second page if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You have it in your hard copy; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, 320.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The last page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- has little wavy line that indicates in addition to a bullet fragment in the body or with the body, there was a cartridge case. I think there was only three of these found.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That case would be 320T. I think that's sufficient for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an example, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If Your Honours want, we can go to the last page of the document. The previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is on the body parts. It's actually the fifth physical page.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And the sign you were mentioning would be on the last column --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very, very --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the very right-hand side. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 375T. Not shown at this moment yet because the bottom of it is not --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We do see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to -- no, we haven't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's either 320 or 375 but both of them have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, 320 --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Which -- yes, we see it now at the top of the English page, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. Okay. Thank you. I think that will suffice for the -- for how to read and interpret this summary chart. Sir, my final question: How did your findings on the human remains found in Tomasica compare to those from other sites in Bosnia you previously worked on as a pathologist? If can you comment about that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were obvious similarities from other sites related to Srebrenica or Croatia or elsewhere. Similarities in that large number of bodies in a mass grave, that most -- the commonest injury in these people was a gun-shot injury caused by a high-velocity weapon. The clothing was of much the same type found, the possessions roughly the same sort of things. So there were similarities with other grave-sites. The differences were the degree of preservation of the bodies in Tomasica, which we've explained. Also by the regular occurrence of injuries to the back of the head. That's what struck us. It was just a recurring feature to find in these cases a gun-shot injury to the back of the head. Certainly not everybody had been killed in that way, but it was a struck us as an unusual feature. These bodies also as in previous grave-sites had injuries caused almost certainly after death by crushing and there were body parts, so in that sense, they were much the same as previous sites. So really the preservation and the preponderance of injuries -- gun-shot injuries to the back of the head were the two things that stood out in these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to start of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know what my answer would be, that we are not ready but we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked whether you were ready to start. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Clark, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First I'm going to put a few general questions to you and then we're going to move on to your report. Tell us, please, how long did you work on the Tomasica case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] For a total of four months, three to four months. I was there from the -- really the start of the case is, I think, in end of November, beginning of December, until about mid-February. There was a period of time at the end of December, beginning of January, when I wasn't there when some cases were carried out, but I saw -- I dealt with the bulk of the cases in this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained this to us today and also in the report that we received from the OTP, it says that you were involved in the third part of the procedure at the mortuary, mentioned on page 2 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we take a look at 65 ter -- well, I haven't written it down. Just a moment, please. It is P7443 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have your report before us here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it has to do with procedure in the mortuary. You gave us an answer today as well, stating that you became involved in what is described here under number 3. You told us that the actions carried out in paragraphs 1 and 2 had already been carried out by other people. How long did this last, that is to say, what was described in paragraphs 1 and 2, opening bags, removing clothing for washing, and then cleaning the bodies themselves, all these things that the anthropologists did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That process was already under way by the time I arrived at the mortuary. Really, from the time that the bodies started arriving from the site into the mortuary, local staff, some of them employed by ICMP, some of them probably not directly employed, but they had started going through the bodies, removing the clothing to wash the bodies so that they could be examined by the anthropology team who would do an inventory of what bones and parts of the body were present, try and assess the sex of the individual from looking at the bones, and sometimes taking a sample at that stage, a bone sample or a tooth sample, for DNA analysis. Once that was completed, the body would be sealed up again in the body bag, awaiting the pathologists to have a look at that in due course, examine the body in due course. We obviously could see the processes going on just in the general course of events, but we had no direct oversight over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise but you did not answer my question. For how long had work already been done, in terms of paragraphs 1 and 2, before you arrived and became involved in the Tomasica case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that probably one to two months. I don't know precisely the date, but it would be of that pat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It would be a fair assessment to say that you had no knowledge whatsoever in terms of what had been done before you arrived there and before you started working on the Tomasica case. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware -- I was aware what procedures had been carried out. I had not witnessed it directly myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How was it that you were aware of the procedures that were applied?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I did arrive, these procedures were still ongoing because there was so many bodies, so I was able to see the bodies being washed and I was informed that a lot of other bodies had already been dealt with. So I could see -- I could see the process. It was still ongoing, and I could see -- similarly I could see the process done by the anthropologists and the records that they kept and the details and the photography done. So I did at least see a substantial number of cases going through these procedures. But, again, only kind of from a distant -- distant point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try to intervene in relation to the procedures that were different from the ones that you had applied earlier on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made unofficial suggestions that this was a different way of doing things, but I realised I was very much the visitor, I had no official role there, that the exercise was now being run by the Bosnian Commission, and that -- well, I had -- I had little influence to change things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us now - briefly - how come you appeared at that location where the autopsies are carried out? You said beforehand that you were a volunteer, and now you said that you were a visitor. Could somebody else have come there as a volunteer or visitor, whoever wished to do so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I've used the word "visitor" loosely. I mean it to say that I was there with permission to be there, but I was not in a position to change anything. The reason I was specifically involved was it was suggested by Professor Sarajlic in Sarajevo that Dr. Durmisevic would probably welcome -- very much welcome my assistance given my past experience and my past interest in this work. So he was very welcoming and made arrangements for the prosecutor to get permission for me to be there. So I wasn't just a casual visitor. I was there with specific permission because of expertise, but at the same time I was conscious that I was there -- I was taking my own -- making my own observations and that the two Bosnian pathologists were doing the official observations for their -- for their purposes for the prosecutor. So -- and nobody else could have been there without permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come you became involved before permission was given? Was this at your own initiative? Did somebody ask you to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly it was my initiative. I was in discussions with Professor Sarajlic about doing research on cases that both of us had been involved in previously in Bosnia, particularly north of Bosnia, and he happened to mention that there was going to be work at the Tomasica site. It was quite a coincidence that it all happened at the same time, and he suggested that it would be good for me to be involved. I was able to be, and so it went on. And that request was made into formal permission for me to be there. So it was a chance circumstances of time and availability.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we say that it was actually your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't have to be there. The work would have gone on had I not been there, certainly. My involvement was also encouraged by both ICMP and ICTY. It just happened that, at that time, at that particular time, it was during a major conference actually here in The Hague involving ICMP and ICTY, so there was direct discussions during the conference, and they both encouraged and facilitated my involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
