utterances.text: In which way did the ICMP and ICTY encourage you and support your participation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness now has answered two similar questions and, of course, we could go to any further details, but unless you have a specific question, I would suggest that you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I think, Your Honour, that it is the first time mentioned involvement of ICTY and encouragement and facilitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's all during discussions, and your previous question was: "Could we say that it was actually your own initiative?" Whereas the previous answer started by saying: "Partly it was my own initiative." So that is an answer to that question. And apparently there have been discussions. The witness says he was interested in view of his research. Others said, Okay, why don't you join us? I mean, what's there -- unless there's any specific matter you would like to add specifically about ICMP encouragement and ICTY, Mr. Clark, if there's such a thing, please tell us that on that specific matter. If not, Mr. Lukic will put his next question to you. And Ms. D'Ascoli is on her feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for the record, that this is not the first time this is mentioned and we can find the references to ICTY and ICMP encouraging Mr. Clark's involvement at page 1 of the report, P7443, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, anything specifically about encouragement to be added?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In fact, ICTY were very keen that I be involved and said that they would be looking for me to produce a report at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before I encourage you to proceed, I would withdraw that, as a matter of fact, and announce that we'll take a break first. Mr. Clark, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Clark, would you agree with me that at the point in time when you went to Tomasica, you had not been issued with any task by the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a verbal -- a verbal task. I had no -- at that stage nothing -- nothing specific in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had not received any written assignments by the BiH Court or the Prosecutor's office, had you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't expect anything from the BiH Court, but -- and my main encouragement was from ICTY to take notes and produce a report, but, again, I had nothing in writing at that stage. Despite asking, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say at that moment. Did you ever receive a task from the Prosecutor's office; and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did receive a written request, an official request, as I recall, not until I'd finished the work there, so afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when you refer to the prosecutor's office, are you referring to the ICTY or of the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the OTP of the ICTY, Your Honour, yes, thank you. I think that Dr. Clark understood it the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is the same anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have your report on the Tomasica grave, 2013 and 2014 report on the findings of autopsies before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our system, it is currently P7443 marked for identification. We have it on our screens. I'm interested in the first page. Let's focus on the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It begins with: "It is my understanding, gained from informal conversations ..." Who did you have these informal conversations with, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was people from ICMP, with Dr. Durmisevic, and other staff present in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to say: "... that the people in this grave were mainly men, that they were primarily or entirely from a group of villages to the west of Prijedor, that they had been killed there in July 1992, than within a few days their bodies had been taken to Tomasica and buried in a deep mass grave." You also say: "I further understand that the following year the grave had been at least partly 'robbed' ..." Did you learn about this from the same people who were included in these informal conversations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it -- yes, it was -- it would have been. I mean, clearly I was there for three to four months. One has chats with people that you meet, come across, and you get little bits of information from time to time, and this was -- so this was the sum of my understanding of the position, and that's -- that's what I'm stressing: It is my understanding of it. I may be factually entirely wrong, but that was my impression that I gained. I can't say specifically who told me the grave had been robbed, but at some stage, I clearly -- I was informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention the robbing of graves, did they tell you that the grave started opening up and that the locals complained and went to the police in Prijedor to report it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do remember being told that at least part of the reason for re-excavating the grave at that stage was because of smell or the water supply being contaminated. That was certainly information that I was aware of. There was -- there was doubt as to when it had happened. I wasn't sure if it was months afterward but somebody said it was the following year, so that's the date I've sort of put there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Thank you. In paragraph 3, you say that: "The exhumation of the grave was carried out from September to November 2013 by the Missing Persons Institute ... with assistance from the International Commission on Missing Persons ..." Do you know who participated on behalf of the Missing Persons Institute?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the main people in charge of the site was Ian Hanson and that he was assisted by other colleagues who had anthropology experience, not saying that they are fully trained anthropologists but they have that experience, and they subsequently came to work in the mortuary as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one second. Mr. Ian Hanson is of the ICMP. I asked you to tell us who was there on behalf of the Missing Persons Institute.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you said ICMP. My mistake. Missing Persons Institute. I really don't know their names. I was aware that they visited the mortuary from time to time as did the people from the state prosecutor's office, but I can't remember specific names. I had no direct involvement with the Missing Persons Institute other than just seeing them around at stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In the same paragraph, you mention that the autopsies were carried out at the facilities at Sejkovaca in Sanski Most. You have explained that the conditions were quite rudimentary. Do you know whose decision it was to perform the autopsies in Sejkovaca?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume it was the state prosecutor who had directed that they be carried out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's but a presumption, Dr. Clark. It's not factual knowledge on your part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just a presumption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- presumption. He must have had, to some extent, the final say. But, yes, it's a presumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page you mention your sources for the drafting of the report. You mention Dr. Dzevad Durmisevic from Bihac and Dr. Nermin Sarajlic from the University of Sarajevo. You say that: "Both will be producing their own formal autopsy reports for the prosecutor." Do you know whether they completed that task and have you ever seen those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen them. I presume -- when I mean prosecutor, I mean the Bosnian state prosecutor. I presume that they have produced them. I have actually not been in contact with them for quite a while, so I'm assuming that they will have produced them by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, it is another presumption. It suffices if you tell us that you simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine. Yes, I do not know if they have produced them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to page 2 now to discuss the procedures in the mortuary. Under this heading: "Procedure in the mortuary," you say that 434 numbers were used in total, 275 of those for bodies, and 125 of those for body parts or general bags. Are body parts and general bags the same category?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Body parts are part of a specific body. General bags can contain bones from more than one body. But, in terms of the body bags in the mortuary, we rather lumped the general bags together with the body parts. We put them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were not whole bodies. Our main concentration was on the whole bodies so we gave them priority, and the other bags were -- were smaller contents and would be dealt with in due course. So they are labelled differently, a GB or a D, but we -- I mean, we kept both of them apart from the main bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, you explain the procedure applied in the mortuary. We have established already that you did not take part in the activities under numerals 1 and 2. You said that you observed the work being carried out while you were present. Under item 1, you say as follows: "Body bag opened ... remains photographed ... clothing removed for washing, and the body ... itself cleaned with a power hose to remove all mud and other debris. In the process, significant numbers of bullets or fragments 'dropped out' ..." First of all, can you define this significant number, or numbers, if you have such data?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an actual figure but I could do because it is the -- in my main table of findings, it would be all the entries which are green and in italics which referred to the bullets which were presented to us separately or accompanying the body but not in the body at the autopsy. So it wouldn't be difficult to total these up, but I would say at least - I don't know - 50, 60 more cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say 50, 60 or more cases. It is over the number of 709. Or is it included in that figure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I'm meaning is the -- we're dealing with effectively 293 cases, autopsies, and in a certain number of these, bullets had already, for want of a better word, dropped out or fallen out of a body by the time they reached the pathologists. Now, as I say, I don't have the exact figure to hand. I could tell you that figure within five minutes, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Perhaps we can use the next break so that can you provide us with that information. But can you tell us now off of the cuff, the 50 or 60 cases, were they included in the figure, or is it on top of that figure so that the final count would be in the area of 750 or 760, or perhaps it doesn't apply to any bullets at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't apply. The 709 are actually physical injuries on the body. Nothing to do whether or not there was bullet present or not. These other bullets or bullet fragments which were found separate from the body, I have merely listed, have made no interpretation of them whatsoever. So they bear no relation to the 709 actually gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, I have a short question to you. You said that within five or ten minutes you could give us the number. Is it just because would you go through the column in which you mentioned them all and then to add them and all the information is already in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic, you can do it yourself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was under wrong impression, then, that there were 709 bullets preserved as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You find in -- I think it was the green ones. And the green regular ones, the witness has explained that, where all the bullets are mentioned, and if you come across a green italics, you know that a cartridge may be involved as well. So, therefore, it is -- everyone who can count from one to a few hundred can do that job, and I think Mr. Clark has provided us with all the information which we need to do such an addition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to emphasise, the -- my interpretation in the report is based -- my interpretation in the report is based on the injuries, not on the bullets fragments. They are just an addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. In the same paragraph you go on to say: "These were documented and photographed and, in due course, collected by police officers as evidence." Were you able to observe in which way these bullets and fragments of bullets were collected?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I observed a few instances of it. And I saw that in the clothes-washer team there was generally two people, one physically washing the body and the other collecting any bullets or documents which -- that they found and putting them into evidence bags and labelling them as such, and they stayed -- they were recorded and then stayed with the general body and were available for us to see at the autopsy. At that stage, they would be probably photographed again by the police and subsequently they would take these samples for evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the autopsies themselves, did you come across bullets or bullet fragments in the bodies themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That question has been answered three times by now, Mr. Lukic. Please proceed. The witness explained that he found bullets in the soft tissue often and that is, therefore, in the bodies. It could not be understood in any other way. So that question has been -- and it's not once but I think it has been dealt with twice or -- perhaps three times is an exaggeration. Would you also, apart from looking at your questions, also carefully consider the answers already given by the witness. Unless I wrongly understood your testimony, Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you're correct, and I can just summarise that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic will put his next question to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise that I did not catch that part of your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The part that Dr. Clark answered, that there were -- that he found actually bullets and bullet parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to ask something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you indicated that your interpretation of the report was based on the injuries only and that there were about 709 injuries. In those injuries, do you include the post-mortem injuries that happened in the grave or is it just the pre-mortem injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is simply the pre-mortem gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 709 refer just to pre-mortem gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I apologise, I was looking at the B/C/S interpreter, waiting for them to conclude their interpretation. I apologise for the breaks that I make, but as you may have become used to it, it is the reality of this Tribunal. Would you agree with me that it is a fact that a bullet remained in the body, confirming that it came from a distance, thus losing velocity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that's one interpretation. If it is a whole bullet, an intact bullet, yes, that would be -- that could be one interpretation. Another interpretation could be that it had come through something or somebody else beforehand and thus lost its energy as well. But that's just for the intact bullets. The bulk of the bullets that we found were actually just small fragments, which is what you would expect, that you would expect these fragments to remain in the body because the bullet has broken up on hitting bone. And bullet fragments, they've lost all their energy, then they stay -- or a substantial amount of them will stay in the body. So, yes, you're right about an intact bullet. You've got to wonder why that has not passed right through the body, but, in fact, most of the specimens we found were fragments of bullets, which you would expect to stay in the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's fragments, could they be the result of the bullet hitting a different surface and then afterwards they were found in this body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically that could account for some of them, but I somehow think that's -- but far more likely is that they are fragments from a bullet which has entered that body in a solid state and broken up in that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, earlier you asked a question about shots being fired from a distance. Could you be more specific as to what distances you have on your mind. Are you talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have specific distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but I didn't mention it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it may make a difference whether you call 30 metres from a distance or whether you call 800 metres from a distance. And -- because I do not know, Dr. Clark, whether this is within your expertise, but you talked about the energy with which a bullet enters a body and what the effect then is. Are you able, and please also tell us when you're not able -- how much energy the bullet loses flying in the air until reaching its target, because if we're talking about a distance and whether that would change anything, would, for example, 30 or 50 metres considerably reduce the energy with which a bullet would hit a body? If can you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it would. I think when we're talking about a distance being the explanation of why a bullet is still in the body, we're talking about probably hundreds of metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hundreds of metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The velocity -- a bullet will travel -- and probably a lot more than that. A bullet will travel a long distance but eventually it's got to come to a stop somewhere, but we're talking about a long way, probably several hundred metres. 30 or 50 metres is -- would have -- the effect would be no different to somebody standing within a metre. The same level of energy would still hit the -- hit -- it would still hit the body with that same amount of energy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I meant to suggest a distance of 300 metres. That is how a bullet would use its impact and would no longer have the energy to go through a body. Would that correspond to your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly not my expertise. I understood that the figure was a good bit higher than that. It would have -- these bullets can travel a lot further than 300 metres. And I think it's only a lot further than that then it would actually lose energy just because of the distance of flying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that they would lose power, but the moment when they can no longer penetrate a body, that happens if they were fired at a distance that is greater than 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my understanding, but I think I'm getting out of the -- my area of expertise, and I wouldn't like to comment any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one follow-up question, and please tell us as well if you consider the question to be beyond your field of expertise. You're talking about high-velocity projectiles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a range, the one flying even faster than the other ones, or is it all more or less the same, if we're talking, for example, about rifle ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some rifles will fire -- will be able to fire a bullet further than others, certainly. I cannot give you the figures, but some weapons are clearly more powerful than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that may impact on the energy still available when hitting a body and, therefore, also whether that energy would be sufficient to leave the body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. But it is my general understanding, and I stand to be corrected, that we're speaking about distances of probably 1.000 metres or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, would you agree with me that the fact that a bullet was found in a body does not necessarily mean that that bullet has to do with the wounding of that particular body, if the bodies were found in mass grave, that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could certainly be the case if the remains were reduced to a skeleton and which you could get transfer of bullets from one body to another. In these cases, we found bullets embedded in bone or soft tissue, a frequent occurrence, so to my mind, that could not have come from -- it must have reached that body as a primary action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again, this witness has told us extensively about how under the specific circumstances in this mass grave that he often was able - not always - often was able to reconstruct or to find the track of the bullet and that sometimes, if the bodies were more skeletonised, that you would not be able to do that. So that is, as far as I understand, the answer to your question, which the witness has already given but was kind enough to now give again. Unless I misunderstood that the gist of your previous answers and your present answer is more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic, and please keep in mind what the report says and what the witness has told us already, rather than to elicit again the same evidence from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask Your Honour to tell me where we have in the report or in the answers the answer about movement of bullets from one body to another. I didn't find it. Maybe I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness tells us that in skeletonised bodies that the bodies [sic] just drop out, that implicitly says -- but I was mainly focusing on the distinction the witness has made between where the bullets were found in the soft tissue, which would make it possible to track the trajectory in the body, and others which just dropped out. Now, if I have ten bodies skeletonised in a heap, if a bullet drops out, it doesn't take much imagination that it may end up in the area of the skeleton of the body next under -- or under that body. That is implicit already from the answer of the witness, but I mainly focused on that he explained to us the reconstruction of the -- and even tell us what the body -- what the track of the bullet in the body was, and that was part of your question as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also actually do cover that point in the last paragraph of page 4, in the end of the third line. Or my third line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we see that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it's really the fourth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're talking about fragments held in place in tissues rather than falling out or into the skeletonised remains.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's -- that's actually part of your answer, not part of my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you had -- you had said that there was no reference to the possibility of bullets falling out of one body into another and I'm just saying that clearly I have considered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, I think what happened is that I said that you had testified about the matter before you gave answers to the questions put by Mr. Lukic. I referred both to your testimony and to the report, and then Mr. Lukic asked me to tell him where it was in the report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I then was unable to immediately locate where it is in the report and referred primarily to your testimony. But now you have assisted me in saying where it is found in your report as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could fragments of bullets and bullets be moved during post-mortem injuries and because of the crumbling of the soil and the like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly in a few cases where the body was reduced to a skeleton, but it would have no influence on bullets which were in tissues or in the bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now talking about the information used in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2, where we've already been. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is that section -- but actually now I'd like to ask you something about a paragraph that is the first paragraph on the third page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version, it is the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you say here is that you had the opportunity to visit Tomasica, although not until the middle of December 2013, by which time all the bodies had been removed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, was the grave-site covered with water?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was still water in one part of it, in the deepest part. It was actually -- there was snow on the ground, and it was frozen water. So there was some water in the deepest part. I can't remember specifically which section it was, but there was some.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Below that there's a heading that says: "Tomasica grave-site." You say the following: "I was informed that Tomasica was an opencast mine and that the grave was in a depression thus created. The bodies within it had been covered by soil and other mine waste, including clay ..." So your understanding, as regards this area, was that there had been mining going on there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you accept my suggestion now, namely that there not been any mining there; rather, waste had been brought there that was not good for processing iron-ore?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still understood that the general Tomasica area was a mine. What happened in that specific area, I don't know. But I'm using the opencast mine in a very general sense, that that whole area was a mine, an iron-ore mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're putting the two as mutually exclusive or are you not? Are you saying it was not a mine but only a deposit of waste?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm telling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say never there was any digging to find minerals or whatever because there still is a possibility - and I do not know whether the witness could tell us anything about this - that you first dig a hole and that you then later fill that hole with waste material which comes from another hole you have dug. It's not entirely clear to me whether you say if it is deposit of material, then it's not a mine; or that you still also in your question - you left it open - that there has been mining activity but then later the holes created by that were then filled by waste material. Which I'm -- it's just unclear to me what you're asking and also, therefore, how we have to evaluate certain answers, apart from this witness knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you want me to testify, but I think I have explanation that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you put your questions in such a way that it is clear what your explanation is and to see whether you can elicit that from the witness, but then have you to put the questions in such a way that the Judges also understand the gist of what you're seeking to establish. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I think that witness told us what he knows. I don't think I can go further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I leave it in your hands how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 5 now in the English version and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we move, Mr. Lukic, I've got a question on this page, if I might. Dr. Clark, during your examination-in-chief, we were shown a table which -- one of which -- whose columns was describing where the body was found in the grave and there was a column saying deposits, spoil, what have you. Looking at this Figure 1 here on this page, I can see the deposits 1s and 2s. Where would be the spoil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's on the next page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The initial table there, Table 1, is only what you can see in that photograph, which is a photograph I obtained from ICMP. If you turn over the page, Table 2 includes everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so you have actually these extra ones, the last four columns, slightly -- it's a grey shading. It's the last four columns that's included there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you, Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I asked to have page 5 in English and page 6 in B/C/S, please. No. There are obviously several versions of this B/C/S version. Can we see the next page, please. Yes, we need the top of the page. We will discuss identifying gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this section, you speak about identifying gun-shot injuries. First, you tell us that the predominant finding in these bodies was gun-shot injury, and you say where the evidence was clear-cut, there was little hesitation in ascribing this as such. In other cases, the qualification "probable" was added, if, for instance, parts were missing. That's what you explained to us today. And, finally, the third category, possible gun-shot injury was used where perhaps there was a simple or more complicated fracture in a bone which could have been caused by a bullet, striking it with reduced energy. Such bullets actually do not cause major damage to the bone; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand that question. Such --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This category of injury that you described as possibly due to a very fast bullet.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a fracture of a bone which was not typically the -- the hole or the shattering which we so often saw, and it could have just been a bullet which had perhaps struck the bone with some reduced energy and just hit it sufficient to fracture it but not to shatter it, that is a possibility. But equally it could have been -- that fracture could have been caused by a blunt -- or a heavy blow from something, whatever. I did not count any of these injuries in my overall assessment, so I kind of ignored these, just recorded them, and in the overall calculation of figures didn't use these at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] As for these bullets that you say you did not take into account at all, would it be fair to say that they -- since these are high-velocity bullets, that is to say, they lost their energy since they had traversed most of their path, would it be fair to say that they had been fired in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to make a correction, you talked about bullets. It's -- we're meaning actually injuries rather than bullets. So these were injuries which could -- possibly could have been caused by a bullet but may have been caused some other way. As I say, I ignored them, but if they were caused by a bullet, yes, it could have been from a bullet fired from a long way away, which had lost energy. That's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is our break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Mr. Clark, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Clark, I'd like to put a general question about bones. Actually, about bone trauma. Would it be fair to say that there are three different types of bone trauma: One caused by a blunt instrument; another caused by a sharp object; as well as trauma caused by a projectile?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair analysis, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we say "projectile," it includes both bullet and shrapnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report -- or in the course of your work, rather, you are supposed to determine what is the consequence of a trauma caused by a blunt instrument as opposed to trauma caused by a bullet or a piece of shrapnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that you encounter problems when trying to distinguish the consequences of trauma, in terms of what can be seen on the bones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Distinguish that from what? Any of the other types of bone injuries?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe in my previous question I asked the doctor about determining the consequence of trauma caused by a blunt instrument as opposed to trauma caused by a bullet or shrapnel. Now I was simply asking him whether, in the course of his work, there are problems to be encountered in terms of distinguishing between the consequences on the bones between the two different types of trauma?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the word -- what you mean by the word "consequence," whether you mean -- if you're meaning distinguishing the three types of trauma, that is one thing. Consequence means the effects of that trauma. So I'm not quite sure what you mean by the word "consequences."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Firstly, I'd like to ask you whether it poses a problem in your work to recognise how a certain injury was caused, whether it was a blunt instrument or a bullet or shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what tissues we have available. If we're just looking at a bone, then we can -- we can usually distinguish which is caused by a sharp instrument. It will be a cutting -- a cutting wound --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but my question was blunt instrument or bullet and/or shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not sharp instrument.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there sometimes can be difficulties distinguishing the two. More often it is quite easy to distinguish the two because a bullet will cause quite a distinctive pattern but there is a grey area in which, yes, blunt force can be -- it can be a little difficult to say which is caused by a projectile or blunt force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yourself that in your work it isn't always easy to find an entry round wound that can be ascertained with a sufficient degree of certainty that it was caused by a bullet. If you compare bone injuries, when do you encounter this problem of determining whether the injury was caused by a blunt instrument or by a bullet or shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually when parts of the bone are missing and we cannot piece everything together, that would be the usual situation. If a bone is very shattered, then it is most likely due to a gun-shot injury. If the fracturing is less, then the distinction becomes more difficult. The situation would be when perhaps there's a single fracture through the bone or perhaps just one or two small parts of the fracture that could be blunt force or it could be part of a projectile injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does it make it even more difficult to distinguish if you need to distinguish between an injury caused by a bullet fragment and the other types of injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a bullet fragment, by definition, will have less energy, so it will hit the bone with probably much the same force as a blunt force injury would -- that's -- that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that post-mortem injuries can also be confusing when trying to ascertain the cause of injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree that the fact that you were unable to assess the distance from which the shot was fired could also influence your determination in terms of the source of injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, yes, if we're speaking about a shot fired from a very long distance away, that -- you would have take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to put one last question regarding this topic by way of a conclusion. Is it correct that, as a scientist, you cannot exclude the possibility that any or some of these people were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can't -- I can't exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question. Mr. Clark, quite a few questions have been put to you on how difficult it is to distinguish between different types of injuries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what we find in your report where you said: I'm unable to establish that it was a gun-shot injury and where you said it is a possible --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- gun-shot injury but could also have been blunt force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. And all these points that have just been put to me would come under this possible category and would be ones which I would not have included in my overall assessment of the cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at page 6. We will now be discussing post-mortem examinations and the specific findings. There you say: "It is up to others to determine how many individuals this entails precisely" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic provide the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on the top of the page in English. "As already noted," it starts there. And then it's: "Precisely how many individuals ..." is under those bullet points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you examined 400 sets of mortal remains but yet you believe that it is for others to determine precisely how many individuals this represented; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the correct page in B/C/S on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is on the screen, Your Honour. It's on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, who is it who should determine the exact figure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps just to clarify, I'm entirely satisfied that there was at least 275 individual people here. In fact, I'm satisfied that it was 293 people based simply on looking at the bodies and recognizing that -- is it -- that's a separate from that person, from that person, from that person. The problem comes with the body parts. Now some of these body parts will belong to some of the bodies that we saw. Some will not and will be a part of a completely different individual, perhaps one of the bodies that had been removed in the robbing. That would be only determined by DNA analysis. And I suspect that with DNA analysis and being able to match up some of these body parts, the actual number of individuals represented - and that's an important word "represented" - in that Tomasica site will probably be higher than 293. From a pathologist point of view, I'm just restricting myself to the physical individuals that I can see, 293. It may be that there are more people represented in that grave-site, but I'm not basing any analysis on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was not your role to determine the number of people involved; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't my role, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I would like to ask for page 7 in the B/C/S version, whereas we should remain on the same page in the English, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that page, we find the title: "Demographics." There you discuss the number of males and females, as well as four sets of remains that were not positively identified as belonging to either sex.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next, you have a breakdown in the table to those who were under 20, the number being 22 individuals; then aged 20 to 35, 37 individuals; 35 to 50, 78 individuals; and over 50, seven individuals. In your view, who is an adult?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my interpretation. I've taken anybody over 20 as an adult. The anthropologists may have a slightly different definition. They talk about sub-adults which may be down as 14, 15, or lower, I don't know. This is my wording. And I've just specified it rather than calling them adults. Well, sorry, when I talk about adult unspecified, that it's clearly somebody who appears to be over the age of 20 but we can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say, therefore, that is your own interpretation, your own categorisation. Is it correct, Doctor, that it is difficult to establish the age of people older than 30 because their bones change very slightly after the age of 30?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that any assessment made by an anthropologist in terms of an individual's age could vary significantly and that it frequently depends on comparisons with other populations not originating from the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Although I gather that more experience has been gained over the years from the Balkans populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 7 in English next and 8 in the B/C/S. In the B/C/S, we need the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you discuss clothing and possessions. You describe what people wore, for the most part. Towards the end, you conclude -- we'll get to the conclusion. Just one second. In any case, in the first paragraph, you enumerate clothing items, and you say jerseys, sweatshirts, long- or short-sleeve shirts, sports shirts, T-shirts, trousers, tracksuit tops and trousers, some had outdoor jackets. Would you agree with me that this would not be customary for the area of Prijedor in July? People would simply not be wearing such clothes, unless they were preparing themselves to spend their night outdoors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's true for some of them. But in amongst that description of all the clothing, there were some people with very light clothing, indeed, just a T-shirt, perhaps shorts. Most people, as I recall, just had a shirt rather than any jerseys. But it's fair to say that some had certainly an excess for clothing for that region in July, yes. But that was the exception. That was the exception. And most people just had what you would call ordinary clothing. Particularly the fact there were lots of T-shirts and shorts, et cetera, would suggest a summertime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is all contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is all contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was would that show that somebody was prepared to sleep outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Isn't that asking for speculation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- you said: "Would you agree with me that this would not be customary ..." What exactly did you refer to when you referred to "this"? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This type of clothing, that that many -- that amount of clothing on somebody in July in Prijedor is not customary. The temperatures are around 30 Celsius at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this the witness -- expert to testify about clothing of people in a certain region?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman testified about clothing and draw conclusions based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So let me just read it again. Because apparently you're referring to the line - and I now better understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's, yeah, paragraph 1, under the clothing and possessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two lines there, the first one describing more or less in general what kind of clothing was found. And then there's a description of excessive clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see what you're -- what you read to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I read the first part, Your Honour, and that was according to me excessive also. Jackets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now -- first of all, in the first line - but, Mr. Clark, please correct me when I'm wrong - there's a general description of what kind of clothing was found, irrespective of how many of such clothes were worn by an individual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that it was the second -- then it follows slightly later, a portion which is talking about an excessive amount of clothing on one person. Mr. Lukic, if you read the first one, then -- and that exactly explains why I asked you what you referred to as "this," but you were referring to whatever was said about what you considered excessive, although the witness has not qualified it as such, and you did not read that part where the witness clearly says that he considered that to be excessive clothing that. That confused me quite a bit, but it's now clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hadn't read it yet. I intended to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't make the question any less unclear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you state your opinion here that you believed such clothes to be excessive when you came upon several layers of clothes on a body. For example, more than one pair of trousers; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have already said that. Today would you be of the opinion that in July in Prijedor it is customary for one to wear a sweater, a woollen shirt, or outdoor jacket?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been in Bosnia in the summertime. I know it gets very hot. I know that some summer days can get cold as well, and it depends on what time of day it is, of course. But generally to me, as I've tried to emphasise, the clothing was light clothing. Yes, some people did have a jersey on, some did have a suit jacket, but that -- they were far fewer in number than people who would be just wearing ordinary light outdoor clothing. I mean, you only look at today, similar temperatures, you would see a range of clothing worn by people in the same sort of temperatures. So it depends on what people were specifically doing. But I read no more into it than the clothing looked generally light clothing, but there were a small number of people who I was surprised at the amount of clothing that they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you quantify that; namely, how many people had clothing that is inappropriate for the month of July in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a figure. Again, I could look through the -- my files. I would have thought if it was anything -- anything more than about 20 people, I think that would be an upper estimate. I think it was really quite a small number of people had excessive clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to put to the witness that in his report he said that it is inappropriate for the month of July in Prijedor, it's not correct. He didn't say so. Nothing can be found in that respect in the report you were citing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I read that, I meant that it seemed that some were wearing an excessive amount of clothing. That is to say, several layers of clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. And you should have put that to the witness and not that it was inappropriate for -- especially for the time, it is a special occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] In the English version, page 7. I think that we're already there. And then page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You refer to six cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version, it's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say in six cases, the clothing showed signs of burning. Would you agree with me that this might indicate shrapnel or shell injuries sustained by these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing to suggest that. I would have anticipated that if this was caused by shrapnel, then there would be evidence of shrapnel in the bodies. There are many other reasons why that clothing could show burning. Shrapnel would be a very low -- low down on my priority of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree at least that a conclusion would depend on a pathologist's interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, interpretation of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The traces that you found.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all -- all I can say, that we saw clothing which had signs of burning on it, I don't know what has caused that. But it certainly did not immediately come to me that this -- this indicated shrapnel damage and there was nothing else to support that in terms of other holes in the body. You know, shrapnel does more than perhaps setting off of burning. It would cause very irregular holes in the clothing. You would expect to impact into the bodies. No signs of that. No sign of that at all. So all I've said, there is some burning there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The clothing you examined had already been removed from the bodies -- or, rather, did you examine the clothing at all; and, if, so how did you go about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the body -- you're correct, the clothing had already been removed from the body. The clothing was in a bag within the body bag after it had been washed. And at the end of autopsy we always laid out the clothing, looked at it in detail, photographed it, and made any comments. So, yes, we -- pathologists always saw the clothing after it had been cleaned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Our time is up for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Lukic, again, the last question, if you look at page 7 and even the photographs and the description, the question whether this witness examined the clothing at all is already answered there. And, therefore, a useless question if not further specified in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was specified in the first part, but I didn't want to jump into the conclusions so I gave the doctor more space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- Mr. Clark, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.30 in this same courtroom. And I again instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, either given already now or in the recent past in this case. Well, recent past. At least in the past in this case, and any testimony still to be given tomorrow. You may follow the usher.
